learningObjective: Distinguish the intended uses of FP8 E4M3 and E5M2 formats and their trade-offs.

canonicalClaims.claim: E4M3 (4-bit exponent, 3-bit mantissa) offers higher precision at narrower range, typically used for weights/activations; E5M2 (5-bit exponent, 2-bit mantissa) offers wider range at lower precision, typically used for gradients. Both are 8-bit formats requiring per-tensor or per-block scale factors.
conditions: The workload runs on Hopper (sm_90) or later Tensor Cores with FP8 support.
Frameworks (e.g., Transformer Engine) manage scale factors.
nonImplications: Does not imply FP8 always matches BF16 accuracy without scale management.
Does not imply Ampere Tensor Cores support FP8 kernels.

misconceptions.claim: FP8 handles the full training dynamic range without any scaling.
misconceptions.whyWrong: FP8's exponent range is much smaller than FP16 or FP32; scale factors are essential for correct training and inference.

misconceptions.claim: FP8 Tensor Cores are available on Ampere via a driver update.
misconceptions.whyWrong: FP8 Tensor Cores are Hopper (sm_90) and Ada (sm_89) hardware features; drivers cannot add them to Ampere.

misconceptions.claim: E4M3 and E5M2 have different total bit widths.
misconceptions.whyWrong: Both are 8-bit total; the difference is in exponent/mantissa split.

misconceptions.claim: E4M3 is always preferred over E5M2 because it has more precision.
misconceptions.whyWrong: For gradients with wide dynamic range, E5M2's wider exponent is essential; E4M3's narrower range can lose values.

implementationFacts: NVIDIA Transformer Engine automates FP8 scaling with the `DelayedScaling` recipe.
E4M3 dynamic range: roughly ±448 with subnormals; E5M2: roughly ±57344.
performanceScenarios: H100 FP8 Tensor Core peak throughput ~2× BF16 peak throughput.
LLM training with FP8 typically reports 1.5-1.8× wall-clock speedup vs. BF16 baseline.
